subject: Quant
topic: Time and work IV — mixed tiers
description: Time-and-work problems: efficiency ratios, alternate days, leaving partway

questions.stem: If 12 men complete a job in 8 days, in how many days will 16 men complete it?
questions.explanation: Total work = 12 × 8 = 96 man-days. With 16 men: time = 96/16 = 6 days. INVERSE PROPORTION: more men, less time. SHORTCUT FORMULA: M₁D₁ = M₂D₂ → 12×8 = 16×D₂ → D₂ = 6. EXTENSION: M₁D₁H₁/W₁ = M₂D₂H₂/W₂ (also include hours/day + work units when those vary). KEY ASSUMPTION: equal efficiency across men. Real-life caveat: adding too many workers can SLOW progress (BROOKS' LAW in software engineering: 'adding manpower to late project makes it later'); coordination overhead grows.

questions.stem: A can do work in 10 days, B in 15 days. Together how long?
questions.explanation: Combined rate = 1/10 + 1/15 = 3/30 + 2/30 = 5/30 = 1/6 per day. Time = 6 days. SHORTCUT FORMULA: T = (T_A × T_B)/(T_A + T_B) = 10×15/(10+15) = 150/25 = 6. INSIGHT — combined time always LESS than either individual time. LCM METHOD: total work = LCM(10,15) = 30 units; A = 3 units/day, B = 2 units/day, combined = 5 units/day → 30/5 = 6 days. INSIGHT — useful when ratio of individual times has clean LCM. SAME logic for: PIPES + CISTERNS, multi-CPU computing, parallel pipelines.

questions.stem: A is twice as efficient as B. Together they finish in 12 days. A alone takes:
questions.explanation: Efficiency ratio A:B = 2:1 → time ratio inverse = 1:2 → A's time : B's time = 1:2. Combined: 1/A + 1/B = 1/12 → 1/A + 1/(2A) = 1/12 → 3/(2A) = 1/12 → A = 18 days; B = 36 days. Verify: 1/18 + 1/36 = 2/36 + 1/36 = 3/36 = 1/12 ✓. SHORTCUT — when A is k times faster: A's time = combined × (k+1)/k. Here k=2: A = 12 × 3/2 = 18. INSIGHT — useful for percentage-efficiency problems. SAME LOGIC: A 50% more efficient than B → A:B = 3:2 efficiency = 2:3 time.

questions.stem: A + B can do work in 12 days; B alone in 30. A alone:
questions.explanation: Combined rate = 1/12. B's rate = 1/30. A's rate = 1/12 − 1/30 = 5/60 − 2/60 = 3/60 = 1/20. So A alone = 20 days. INSIGHT — when COMBINED + ONE ALONE are given, find OTHER by SUBTRACTION of rates. Verify: 1/20 + 1/30 = 3/60 + 2/60 = 5/60 = 1/12 ✓. PYQ standard. ALSO: if A + B + C combined rate is given, with A + B's combined and B + C's combined, can find each individually using rate algebra.

questions.stem: A alone in 24 days, B alone in 16 days. A starts; B joins after some days; together they finish in 12 total days. After how many days did B join?
questions.explanation: Let B joined on day x; B works (12−x) days. Total work = 12 × (1/24) [A all 12 days] + (12−x) × (1/16) [B from day x] = 1. → 12/24 + (12−x)/16 = 1 → 1/2 + (12−x)/16 = 1 → (12−x)/16 = 1/2 → 12−x = 8 → x = 4. So B joined after 4 days. SHORTCUT verify: A alone for 4 days does 4/24 = 1/6 of work. Remaining 5/6 by A+B together at rate 1/24+1/16 = 5/48 → time = (5/6)/(5/48) = 8 days. Total = 4+8 = 12 ✓. INSIGHT — ALWAYS set up TOTAL WORK = 1 equation; use linear algebra in time variables.

questions.stem: 20 men can complete work in 30 days. After 10 days, 5 men leave. Total time:
questions.explanation: Total work = 20 × 30 = 600 man-days. After 10 days: 20 × 10 = 200 done; 400 left. With 15 men: time = 400/15 ≈ 26.67 days. Total = 10 + 26.67 ≈ 36.67 days. INSIGHT — when worker count CHANGES PARTWAY, split into stages: (1) Stage 1: original team for x days (work done = M₁ × x); (2) Stage 2: remaining team for y days (= M₂ × y). Total work = constant; solve. CONCEPT: PROJECT MANAGEMENT real-life — workers leaving / joining shifts schedule. Useful for: construction, software projects, harvest-period labour.

questions.stem: If 1 man = 2 women in efficiency, and 5 women complete a job in 24 days, how long do 4 men take?
questions.explanation: 1 man's efficiency = 2 women's. So 4 men = 8 women's worth. Total work in 'woman-days' = 5 × 24 = 120 woman-days. Time for 4 men (= 8 women) = 120/8 = 15 days. SHORTCUT — convert all to a SINGLE UNIT (here 'woman-units') based on efficiency ratio, then use M·D = constant. KEY INSIGHT: efficiency-ratio problems become simple unit-conversion + standard work-rate equations. SAME APPROACH for: gender-mixed crews, machine speed differences, child + adult workers, parallel workers with different output rates.
